To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Q-S 2 interval, which is an index of the electromechanical interval from the beginning of ventricular depolarization to the opening of the semilunar valves, is the most useful interval for the evaluation of the electromechanism in the newborn infant, and that this interval decreases with age during the first week, as does the Q-T interval.
in the healthy newborn the following intervals decrease during the first week after birth: the Q-S 2 interval, the S 1 - S 2 interval and the Q-T interval.
the electromechanical intervals in newborn infants change in predictable ways during the first week after birth, but that these changes do not correlate with changes in heart volume or blood volume.

the electromechanical intervals in newborns are different from those in adults and that the changes in these intervals during the first week are not related to the changes in heart rate or heart volume.

in newborn infants, the Q-S 1 interval is constant and the Q-S 2 and S 1 - S 2 intervals decrease during the first week after birth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electromechanical intervals of the newborn are different from those of older individuals.
the newborn infant has a very short electromechanical interval and a very short electrical systole.
the electromechanical intervals in normal infants are different from those of older individuals and that these differences are not the result of the small heart size of the newborn.

we have demonstrated the feasibility of using a single-photon emission tomography (SPECT) system to image the electrical activity of the heart in a newborn infant.
